newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian rate cut in Dec quarter still seen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian rate cut in Dec quarter still seen.

text.p: Hopes of a near term Australian rate cut remain firmly intact, despite the uneventful passing on Wednesday of what was seen as a quick opportunity of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to again cut the official cash rate.
Only the most optimistic in the market had expected a cut to be delivered this week, with most seeing the late October/early November period as the RBA's best time to ease.
Slowing inflation and wages growth, stalled unemployment and activity and large cuts to government spending are the main factors for those arguing for a fourth quarter cut.
"Because the economy's fairly soft and because inflation is falling, we are expecting the Reserve Bank to ease 50 points," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.

"The economy needs a touch of a jolt -- 50 points wouldn't set the world on fire but it may make the economy move out of its current mediocre phase, so half a percent before Christmas is our near term view."

The latest Reuters survey of economists on the rates outlook, conducted ahead of the RBA board meeting last Tuesday, found 23 of the 32 economists surveyed expected a rate cut, and all expected it to be before the end of calendar 1996.

Only two expected an October cut, while a further eight saw it as a distinct possibility -- however they expected the cut to occur late in October after the release of third quarter inflation and wages data on October 23 and 24 respectively, not straight after the RBA board meeting.
"I think it will come after the data, if it's going to occur," Merrill Lynch chief economist Nigel Douglas said.
"...the wages data will be important because it gives them a comprehensive picture of the wages situation rather than just isolated settlements," he said.
Westpac senior economist John Peters said while a cut on Wednesday could not have been ruled out, it was always low risk.
Instead, he thought the RBA would wait until they had an update on the wages outlook, and received confirmation of the moderating inflation outlook.
"We think they'll have a look at those numbers and if they come in on cue, and if they are continuing to moderate, then they'll move," Peters said, .
"Basically our view still is we'll have a rate cut in November and that'll probably be it for this cycle," he said.

While economists had seen little chance of a rate cut being announced on Wednesday, bank bill futures traders were among the The futures market opens one hour before any RBA announcement on policy is made, and December bill futures opened very strongly on speculation of a cut.
At their strongest, the implied yield on the futures had fallen to 6.51 percent -- almost a full half percent under the official cash rate of 7.00 percent.

They weakened slightly when no cut was forthcoming but by the end of the day were still 40 points under the official rate. But if an easing hasn't happened by the end of 1996, then the odds will start to swing in favour of a tightening from mid-1997 onwards as the next move in monetary policy, economist said
"This is the window of opportunity in our view...if they moved by early in the New Year they won't be moving to cut -- but we think they will," Westpac's Peters said.
